London Buses

Buses, the Tube, changing lines and paying: find your way in a big city.

Road map

Lesson of 55 minutes, timed for 52 minutes. 3 lessons.

  1. Lesson 1 · Oxford Street, warm-up and buses 52 min

    Read the short text about an Oxford Street without buses, gather what we know about London, describe a bus and match lines to landmarks.

Curriculum link

This lesson fits the French modern languages curriculum for vocational schools (2019, common to CAP and bac pro).

Context

Everyday, personal, social and civic life. The curriculum also aims at mobility and intercultural skills.

Cultural topics

  • Geography: big cities, means of transport and networks.
  • Symbolic places: famous monuments, cultural sites.
  • Tourism: travelling, visiting.

Communication tasks

  • CAP, A2: ask for and understand directions, timetables, an announcement in a public place.
  • Bac pro, B1 and above: ask for detailed practical information, understand the presentation of a visit.

Level

In Year 1, CAP students work at A2 and bac pro students at B1. The target at the end of the bac pro is B1+ for the first foreign language.

Mobility and independence

Finding your way in a city you don't know is a fear many students share. Some have never taken an underground train. Others have never left their region.

Reading a map, asking for directions, paying for a journey: these are steps towards independence. They build confidence for a work placement abroad, a school trip or a first job in a big city.

The topic also raises a real question: who can move easily in a city? The price of transport, access for disabled people, the importance of buses for people without a car.

Message to share before the lesson. You have the right to get lost. What matters is knowing how to ask.
Hook · News from 26 October 2026

No more buses on Oxford Street!

Oxford Street is the most famous shopping street in London. From the end of October 2026, a big part of it is closed to cars. Buses can't go there anymore.

The facts

  • Where? From Orchard Street to Great Portland Street, about 900 metres, including Oxford Circus.
  • Which buses? Day routes 7, 94, 98, 139 and 390. Night routes N7, N98, N113, N137 and N207.
  • What happens? Buses take other streets. The new bus stops are 100 to 200 metres away from Oxford Street.
  • How long? First a test period until spring 2027. Then the change can become permanent.

A street full of buses

  • How many red buses can you count?
  • What are the flags above the street? Whose flag is it?
  • Imagine the same street with no buses. What can you see instead? Use: pedestrians, shoppers, trees, benches, it's quieter.
Possible answers

I can count five red buses. The flags are Union Jacks, the flag of the United Kingdom. Without buses, there are more pedestrians and shoppers. It's quieter and the air is cleaner.

For or against?

For

  • Cleaner air.
  • It's safer for pedestrians.
  • More space for events and shops.

Against

  • It's harder for disabled people: the bus stops are further away.
  • Taxis can't drop people off.
  • More traffic in the small streets nearby.

Your turn

  1. Find Oxford Circus on the map in tab 2. Which Tube lines stop there?
  2. Imagine you use a wheelchair. Is this good news for you? Why?
  3. Give your opinion: "I think it's a good idea because…" / "I don't agree because…"
Answers

1. Marble Arch, Oxford Circus, Tottenham Court Road. At Oxford Circus: the Victoria line and the Central line (and the Bakerloo line on the real map). 2 and 3: open answers.

For the teacher. Show the Facebook post as a hook. It takes students from simple description (taking a bus) to a real social question: who does the city belong to? Pedestrians, shop owners, people who can't walk very far?

Warm-up

Look and speak

  1. What can you see in this photo?
  2. Is it day or night? How do you know?
  3. What are the red and white lines in the street?
Possible answers

I can see Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament. It is night: the sky is dark blue and the buildings are lit up. The red and white lines are the lights of cars and buses moving fast.

Where is it?

Match each number with a place: Big Ben, Tower Bridge, Buckingham Palace, King's Cross station, St Paul's Cathedral, the London Eye.

Answers

1. Buckingham Palace 2. Big Ben 3. the London Eye 4. St Paul's Cathedral 5. Tower Bridge 6. King's Cross station

What do you know about London? Name a monument, a colour, a means of transport.

1. Buses: see London from the top deck

Then and now: London still runs red double-decker buses through the streets around Oxford Street. In this photo, a Routemaster on route 390 is at work on New Oxford Street.

Describe the photo

Work in pairs. Use: in the foreground, in the background, on the left, on the right, there is, there are.

  • How many buses can you see? What colour are they?
  • What is the black car in front of the buses?
  • What can you see in the background?
  • What is the weather like?
Model answer

In the foreground, there are two red double-decker buses and a black cab, a London taxi. In the background, on the right, there is Big Ben, the clock tower. On the left, there is the Palace of Westminster, where the Parliament meets. The sky is blue: it is a sunny day.

London has hundreds of bus routes. Some go past famous monuments, so you can visit the city for the price of a bus ticket.

Three routes for sightseeing

RouteYou can see…
11Westminster, Trafalgar Square, the Strand, St Paul's Cathedral
24Camden Town, Trafalgar Square, Whitehall, Westminster
15Trafalgar Square, St Paul's Cathedral, the Tower of London

Routes can change: check the TfL website before the lesson.

Good to know

  • No cash on buses. Pay with a contactless card, a phone or an Oyster card.
  • On the bus, you tap in only once, when you get on.
  • Press the red button to stop the bus.

Exercise

You want to see St Paul's Cathedral and the Tower of London on the same bus. Which route do you take?

Answer

Route 15.

Last stop: Tower Bridge

You get off route 15 at the Tower of London. Look at the photo.

  • What is the name of this bridge? What river does it cross?
  • Compare the old buildings and the new ones. Use: old, modern, tall, made of glass, made of stone.
  • One skyscraper looks like a vegetable. Which one? Its nickname is "the Gherkin" (un cornichon).
Possible answers

It is Tower Bridge. It crosses the river Thames. The bridge is old and made of stone. Behind it, the skyscrapers of the City are modern, very tall and made of glass. The round building on the right is the Gherkin.

Rush hour

Why is the bus blurred? Is it a good time to take the bus? Use: rush hour, traffic, crowded, fast, slow.

Possible answer

The bus is blurred because it is moving fast. It is the evening, maybe rush hour: there is a lot of traffic and the buses are crowded.

2. The Tube: lines and colours

Then and now: in 1905, a poster invited Londoners to take the Central London Railway, today the Central line, and to avoid the anxiety of the streets above.

The London Underground opened in 1863. It is the oldest underground railway in the world. Londoners call it "the Tube". Each line has a name and a colour.

Simplified map

A very simplified map: stations in between are not shown. Give students the real TfL map too.

Four lines to know

LineUseful stations
VictoriaKing's Cross, Oxford Circus, Green Park, Victoria
CentralOxford Circus, St Paul's, Bank
JubileeGreen Park, Westminster, Waterloo
DistrictSouth Kensington, Victoria, Westminster, Tower Hill

Exercise

  1. Which station is the closest to Big Ben?
  2. Which line goes to St Paul's?
  3. What colour is the Victoria line?
Answers

1. Westminster. 2. The Central line. 3. Light blue.

3. Changing lines

Sometimes there is no direct line. You need to change. Look at the map and find the station where two lines meet.

Model dialogue

Tourist: Excuse me, how do I get to Big Ben from King's Cross?

Staff: Take the Victoria line southbound to Green Park.

Tourist: And then?

Staff: Change at Green Park and take the Jubilee line to Westminster. It's one stop.

Tourist: How long does it take?

Staff: About fifteen minutes.

Tourist: Thank you very much!

Useful phrases

  • Take the … line to …
  • Change at … for the … line.
  • Get off at … It's … stops.
  • Is this train going to …?

Exercise: give the directions

  1. From Tower Hill to the museums in South Kensington.
  2. From Waterloo (London Eye) to the Tower of London.
  3. From King's Cross to St Paul's Cathedral.
Answers

1. Take the District line westbound to South Kensington. No change!

2. Take the Jubilee line to Westminster, then change for the District line eastbound to Tower Hill.

3. Take the Victoria line to Oxford Circus, then change for the Central line eastbound to St Paul's.

4. Paying for your journey

You can't buy a ticket on a London bus. Most people pay with a contactless bank card or a phone. You can also use an Oyster card, a blue card you top up with money.

Prices in 2026 (pay as you go)

JourneyPrice
Bus, one journey£1.75
Bus, maximum per day£5.25
Tube, zone 1, peak time£3.10
Tube, zone 1, off-peak£3.00
Tube and bus, zones 1-2, maximum per day£8.90

Fares from March 2026. Bus fares were frozen until at least 5 July 2026: check tfl.gov.uk before the lesson.

Three rules

  • Hopper fare: change buses as many times as you want in one hour, for £1.75.
  • Daily cap: after a certain amount, you pay nothing more for the rest of the day.
  • Tap in and tap out in the Tube. If you forget to tap out, you pay the maximum fare.

Maths in English

Sam takes the bus four times in one day. How much does he pay? Why?

Answer

4 × £1.75 = £7.00, but the daily cap is £5.25, so he pays £5.25.

Pair work: at the ticket office

Student A is a French tourist. Student B works for TfL. Then swap roles.

Student A

You are at King's Cross. You want to visit the London Eye.

  • Ask for directions.
  • Ask how much it costs.
  • Ask if you can pay with your phone.

Student B

Use the map. Give clear directions.

  • Victoria line to Green Park.
  • Change for the Jubilee line to Waterloo.
  • Explain contactless and the price.
Variation. Replace the London Eye with St Paul's, then the Tower of London. Stronger students add a problem: "The Jubilee line is closed today."

Written test

Part 1: Vocabulary (5 points)

Complete with: bus stop, change, tap out, fare, southbound.

  1. Wait for the bus at the …
  2. Don't forget to … when you leave the station.
  3. The … for one bus journey is £1.75.
  4. Take the train going south: it's the … train.
  5. There is no direct line, so you need to …

Part 2: Map reading (5 points)

Using the map, write the directions from Victoria to Bank.

Part 3: Writing (10 points)

Your friend is going to London. Write a message (60 to 80 words). Explain how to go from King's Cross to Big Ben, and how to pay.

Answer key and marking

Part 1. 1. bus stop 2. tap out 3. fare 4. southbound 5. change

Part 2. Take the Victoria line to Oxford Circus, change for the Central line to Bank. Accept any logical route.

Part 3. Correct directions (4), payment explained (3), language and linking words: first, then, after that (3).

Speaking

Talking alone (1 to 2 minutes)

Present your perfect day in London. Say which monuments you visit, which lines or buses you take, and how much you spend.

Interaction

The teacher plays a lost tourist. The student helps with the map.

Assessment criteria

  • The message is clear.
  • The directions are correct.
  • The student uses the phrases from the lesson (take, change at, get off).
  • The student keeps the conversation going and asks questions.
Going further. The game "A Day in London" lets students act out these situations in a real story.

Exam practice

This lesson prepares the oral assessment: present a project, then answer questions.

Sample task

Your class is going on a school trip to London. Present a one-day programme: places to visit, transport, budget.

What the student prepares

  • Three monuments and the closest stations.
  • A route with at least one change.
  • A small transport budget, with the daily cap.
  • Two questions the examiner could ask, and the answers.

Student sheet

I can…

  • name four Tube lines and their colours;
  • find the closest station to a monument;
  • give directions with one change;
  • explain how to pay on a bus and in the Tube;
  • say what I think about a street without cars.

Key sentences

  • Take the Victoria line to Green Park.
  • Change at Green Park for the Jubilee line.
  • Get off at Westminster.
  • You can't pay cash on the bus.
  • Don't forget to tap out!
